findings.title: Section 54234: real statute, but it doesn't clearly explain the NOA delay
findings.summary: The research files said Gov Code Section 54234(a)(2) freezes the Y-1 notice during the lawsuit. The statute's text extends completion deadlines for pre-2019 deals; it does not say a new notice must wait. Why CRA/LA is holding the notice is unconfirmed.
details: The statute says the specified deadlines are extended when the disposition of the property, the agency's right or ability to dispose of it, or a development project proposed for it is the subject of a judicial challenge. The extension runs to six months after that litigation finally concludes.
- The file argues that the Angels Landing Partners case (24STCV32173) triggers the extension because it involves both the disposition and a development project proposed for the property
- Result: disposition deadlines, including NOA issuance, are extended until six months after the litigation concludes
- The file calls the delay legally defensible, but notes CRA/LA has not publicly explained it

- Checked Sept 27, 2026 against the official text: Section 54234 lets deals under an exclusive negotiating agreement signed before Sept 30, 2019 finish under the old law by Dec 31, 2027, and extends that completion deadline to six months after any litigation ends. It does not say a new Notice of Availability must wait. The extension language is not in paragraph (a)(2), which covers the Metro North Hollywood project.
- Angels Landing's exclusive negotiating agreement was signed March 28, 2018, so the grandfathered deal may be what the lawsuit keeps alive. That link is our inference.

findings.title: Remaining steps before Y-1 NOA can issue
findings.summary: According to the file, the Y-1 disposition can move forward only after the litigation reaches a final conclusion, a six-month period then passes, and the NOA is issued, which opens the 60-day window for letters of interest.
details: - Step 1: the litigation reaches a final conclusion, by settlement or judgment
- Step 2: the six-month extension period under §54234 runs
- Step 3: the NOA is issued to all qualified recipients at the same time (HCD, local public entities, and registered affordable housing developers / housing sponsors)
- Step 4: the 60-day window for written letters of interest begins, and if any are received, at least 90 days of good-faith negotiation follow
The file gives no trial date or settlement timeline, so it cannot say when the NOA might issue.
- Caution: these steps assume Section 54234 blocks the notice. The statute's text does not say so (see disp-004).

findings.title: SLA notice rule: all qualified entities notified at once
findings.summary: Under Gov Code §§54222/54223, the agency sends a written Notice of Availability to HCD, local public entities, and registered housing sponsors at the same time, and every qualified entity gets the same 60-day window to respond.
details: - The NOA must go out at least 30 days before any disposition, by email or certified mail
- Recipients: HCD, local public entities with jurisdiction, and certified affordable housing developers ('housing sponsors') on HCD's registry
- Qualified entities have 60 calendar days to express interest in writing
- The notice is not sequential: no recipient gets an earlier or longer window
- If no letters of interest arrive, the file says the property can move to public auction

findings.title: Affordable housing gets priority among multiple respondents
findings.summary: If more than one qualified entity expresses interest, the agency must give first priority to affordable housing (Gov Code Section 54227(a)) (unless the property is designated for parks or recreation), and then negotiate in good faith for at least 90 days.
details: There is no tiered order that gives cultural organizations or any other party first choice. When several qualified entities respond, affordable housing gets priority.
- Good-faith negotiation must last at least 90 days (Gov Code §54223)

- HCD's definition of good faith: serious effort, reasonable meeting times, prompt responses, and consideration of reasonable offers. Refusing to meet, ignoring offers, or demanding large departures from the NOA do not count.
- Example (Sacramento, 3625 Fong Ranch Road, declared March 2, 2021): two affordable housing entities responded, and the city chose Anton DevCo's proposal because it offered the most affordable units
- Corrected Sept 27, 2026: the research files cited Sections 54222/54223 for this rule. The priority rule is in Section 54227(a). Section 54223 covers the 90-day negotiation.

findings.title: Affordability covenant: 15% or 25% of units, 55/45-year terms
findings.summary: When 10 or more residential units are built on surplus land, at least 15% must be affordable, or 25% if the receiving entity is dedicated to affordable housing. The covenant lasts 55 years for rentals and 45 years for ownership housing.
details: - Tribal trust lands: 25% affordable for 50 years
- Income target: lower-income households, described as 70–80% of AMI depending on the provision (the file flags this as unresolved)
- Affordable cost is defined under Health & Safety Code §50052.5 (housing cost) and §50053 (rent). Lower-income is defined under §50079.5.
- The deed restriction must be recorded before the land use entitlement, runs with the land, and binds all successors
- It can be enforced by local public entities, HCD, housing developers, qualified entities, community land trusts, and California Indian Tribes

findings.title: SLA violation penalties: 30% first, 50% subsequent
findings.summary: Under Gov Code §54230, a first violation carries a penalty of 30% of the greater of the final sale price or fair market value, and later violations carry 50%. There is also a broad private right of action.
details: - The penalty applies when an agency disposes of land in violation after HCD has notified it
- HCD issues a findings letter about 30 calendar days after a complete submission, and the agency then has at least 30 days to correct the problem or adopt an explanatory resolution
- Low-income individuals, certified affordable housing developers, advocacy groups, and other interested parties can sue for injunctive relief, penalties, and attorney fees
- Enforcement activity: HCD has issued 816+ letters since 2021, and the file credits the program with 28,419 housing units (16,772 affordable)

findings.title: Successor agencies such as CRA/LA are subject to the SLA
findings.summary: Successor agencies to former redevelopment agencies fall within the SLA's definition of 'local agency'. There is no blanket successor-agency exemption, so the Y-1 disposition goes through SLA procedures unless a standard exemption applies.
details: - Standard exemptions include agency-to-agency transfers for government use, transfers to California Indian Tribes or community land trusts, small parcels (<5,000 sq ft, or <10,000 sq ft under certain conditions), former rights-of-way, property with existing affordability restrictions, and certain park/recreation land
- Each disposition is reviewed separately for exemption eligibility
- Related precedent: Anderson v. City of San Jose (2019, Sixth District Court of Appeal) held that charter cities, including Los Angeles, are subject to the SLA

findings.title: AB 1734: LA-only charter city exemption through 2034
findings.summary: AB 1734 (Jones-Sawyer, signed in 2024) creates an SLA exemption for charter cities with more than 2.5 million people, a category only Los Angeles currently meets. It covers land used for navigation centers, supportive housing, youth transitional housing, and affordable housing, and sunsets January 1, 2034.
details: - Conditions: a compliant housing element, an HCD 'pro-housing' designation, and specific development requirements
- Covered uses: low-barrier navigation centers, supportive housing, youth transitional housing, affordable housing

- Other 2024 bills: SB 747 and AB 480 clarified what 'participating in negotiations' means (RFP/RFQ issuance, lease negotiations, and ENAs are excluded) and added agency-use exemptions for ports, broadband/wireless sites, and waste-facility buffer sites
- The file does not say whether AB 1734 applies to Y-1, which CRA/LA, not the City, is disposing of

findings.title: Open questions: SLA implementation gaps relevant to Y-1
findings.summary: The file lists unresolved SLA implementation issues. The ones most relevant to Y-1 are unclear HCD enforcement for CRA successor-agency dispositions, the 70% vs 80% AMI targeting question, and how long-term covenants get enforced.
details: - Successor agency guidance: little published guidance exists, and HCD's enforcement approach to CRA-related dispositions is unclear
- Income targeting: provisions refer to 70% or 80% AMI, and HCD has not clarified which applies when
- Good-faith negotiation: the scope is still disputed case by case, and HCD's interpretation is evolving
- Covenant enforcement: it is hard to identify who is responsible for 45–55+ year covenants once the property changes hands
- Deadline pressure: many agencies face the December 31, 2027 extended disposition deadline, which could strain HCD's review capacity
- The file notes there are few published case studies of CRA successor-agency dispositions

findings.title: Arthur Erickson wins 1980 California Plaza master plan competition
findings.summary: Arthur Erickson beat the 'All-Stars' consortium to win the Bunker Hill / California Plaza master plan competition in 1980; the City Council approved the California Plaza Project on January 19, 1982.
details: The competition was announced in 1979. Erickson competed against an 'All-Stars' consortium that included Frank Gehry, Barton Myers, Charles Moore, Cesar Pelli and Lawrence Halprin. By summer 1980 the two were the final contenders, and Erickson was selected by mid-1980.
- 1980: first master plan completed; 1980-1981: second master plan developed
- September 1981: CRA/LA prepared the California Center Environmental Impact Report
- January 19, 1982: LA City Council approved the California Plaza Project for Bunker Hill; construction was slated to begin in fall 1982
- Project scope: 11.2 acres (four downtown blocks), roughly $1.2 billion over 10 years, developer Bunker Hill Associates, on public land obtained from the City

findings.title: CCA holds Erickson's original California Plaza master plan materials
findings.summary: The Canadian Centre for Architecture's Arthur Erickson fonds holds the 1979-1980 competition and master plan materials, including the first and second plans. Access is by appointment only.
details: CCA acquired the fonds directly from Erickson in 1987 and added to it twelve times between 1989 and 2004. Archivists Alexandra Jokinen and Catherine Jacob reprocessed it in 2020-2021. The catalogue reference is AP022.S1.1979.PR07.
- Holdings: the California Plaza Competition and Master Plan (1979-1980) and the California Plaza Phase 2A documentation
- Design development and presentation drawings, slides, composite photographs, models
- Phase 2A includes a 54-storey office tower design plus retail and performance plaza specifications; 18 rolls of transmittal sheets (paving layouts, framing plans, structural steel)
- Inquiries: archives@cca.qc.ca. The drawings that might show how the museum was classified can only be seen in person.

findings.title: New-buyer CEQA paths: Addendum vs. Subsequent EIR vs. new EIR
findings.summary: The file's own analysis sets out three CEQA paths for a new buyer depending on the entitlements' status and how far the project changes. Estimated time to construction-ready ranges from about 20 to 63 months.
details: These estimates are the file's analysis, not official figures.
- Addendum (CEQA Guidelines §15164): minor changes, no new impacts, no public review; 6-12 months, $50-150K. Overall scenario: 20-30 months.
- Subsequent EIR (§15162): substantial changes or new impacts; 45-day minimum circulation; 12-18+ months, $150-400K. Overall scenario: 27-42 months.
- New EIR for a different use with opposition or litigation: 12-24 months, $200-500K. Overall scenario: 33-63 months.
- The file's bottom line: don't rely on the 2022 entitlements; plan for at least 24-42 months

findings.title: The parcel is a residue, not a surplus
findings.summary: Y-1's surplus status is read as evidence of an unfinished redevelopment promise rather than a development opportunity, which recasts affordability as institutional restitution.
details: The Bunker Hill Redevelopment Plan expired and California dissolved redevelopment agencies in 2012 (AB x26), yet CRA/LA still holds residual assets, including Y-1, in 2026. The diagnostic argues the parcel is not planned-but-delayed capacity but a trace of institutional failure.
- Reframes affordability from a public-benefit add-on to restitution for the original residential clearance of Bunker Hill.
- Design implication stated in the file: the project is not completing a legacy but recovering from one.

- The companion reframing table sets 'Legacy Completion (honor 1980 bargain)' against 'Restitution Architecture (acknowledge historical debt)'; other pairs include MOCA-as-anchor vs. occupant unknown, and mixed-use-with-some-affordability vs. housing-first.

- The claim that CRA/LA still holds 168 assets is stated without a named source in the diagnostic (the Key Findings file refers to Y-1 as 'Asset 168'); the Validation Protocol lists it as a claim to verify via a CRA/LA asset list request.

findings.title: Affordability economics invert the project
findings.summary: Moving from Angels Landing's token affordable units to a Surplus Land Act covenant makes housing, not market-rate capture, the structural driver of financing, density and ground-floor programming.
details: The diagnostic argues that a 25% affordable share under a 55-year covenant is not an add-on but a structural inversion of the pro forma.

- File figures: Angels Landing had 13 affordable units in a roughly 1.3M sq ft scheme ('~1%' in the Diagnostic, '~2%' in the Strategic Brief); '240+ housing units' on a 97,631 sq ft parcel; '215 units x 55 years = 11,825 unit-years'. None of these unit counts has a named source, and they are internally inconsistent (240+ vs. 215).

- The '25% minimum' is stated flatly in the Diagnostic. The WebSearch file gives it as 25% if a qualified housing entity pursues the site or 15% if not, and Key Findings gives 25-100% depending on disposition path.
- Design implication stated in the file: the pro forma changes completely when affordability becomes the primary driver.

findings.title: The litigation stall as a multi-year research runway
findings.summary: The file reads the delayed Notice of Availability as a statutory suspension (Gov Code §54234(a)(2)) rather than bureaucratic friction, and recommends using the resulting years for research rather than speed.
details: The diagnostic says the parcel will not move until a court order closes the Angels Landing case and six more months pass, and that the pre-construction years should be spent on archival, legal, geotechnical and financial research.

- Timeline estimates are unverified and conflict with each other: the Diagnostic and WebSearch file give '2028-2030' for groundbreaking, the Strategic Brief shows construction starting Q1 2033 after a 7-year runway, and the WebSearch file estimates settlement approval in '2027-2028'. None has a named source.

- The Diagnostic describes the lawsuit as 'pending as of Sept 2026', but Key Findings and the WebSearch file record a joint settlement stipulation (Sept 10, 2026) and a stay order (Sept 12, 2026). The estimates predate or ignore the settlement.
- Design consequence in the Strategic Brief: early-stage design should be exploratory, not prescriptive, so that constraints come to light before construction.

- Checked Sept 27, 2026: Section 54234's text extends completion deadlines for pre-2019 deals and does not say the new notice must wait, so the 'statutory suspension' reading is an inference (see disp-004).

findings.title: The 'clean slate' is a liability minefield
findings.summary: The lapsed Angels Landing entitlements do not clear the site. A new owner inherits easement, hazard, insurability and CEQA-baseline uncertainties that come before any program decision.
details: The diagnostic lists what a new owner inherits:
- 1983 COREA easements with California Plaza (terms unexamined); the Angels Flight Railway right-of-way (recorded); non-insurable subsurface (Subdivision Map Act).
- Earthquake-induced landslide and liquefaction zones; a 70 ft elevation fall from Olive St to Hill St.
- No recorded Development Agreement to vest approvals; uncertain Final EIR status.

Design implication stated in the file: due diligence is a design activity, not a post-design requirement. The Strategic Brief's risk map rates COREA terms, the landslide zone and Final EIR status as HIGH severity.

findings.title: Restitution-model program mix vs. Angels Landing model
findings.summary: The Strategic Brief proposes a housing-led program with a large affordable share, reduced retail, flexible community/cultural space and a small Bunker Hill history archive.
details: Restitution Model (at a 25% affordability floor): 300 market-rate units; 215 affordable units; 50K sq ft retail; 20-30K sq ft flexible community/cultural space; 3-5K sq ft local history archive/exhibition (Angels Flight, Bunker Hill history).

- Ground floor shifts from a retail/cultural showcase to affordable-housing integration, community access and local history documentation; the tower is framed as a housing provider with civic responsibility.

- Financing: a cross-subsidy model (market-rate units subsidize affordable rents) plus an HCD/CalHFA permanent loan, tax-exempt bonds with LIHTC, a CRA/LA land value credit, and possibly an affordable-housing nonprofit partner.

- Caveat: the brief's 'Angels Landing Model' baseline (600 market-rate units, 13 affordable, 150K sq ft retail, 70K sq ft MOCA cultural space, and a '12-story tower' in Shift #4) has no named source and conflicts with Key Findings, which describes 854 ft and 494 ft towers with 180 condos, 252 rentals and 515 hotel rooms.

sources.title: Y-1 Strategic Brief, Design Shift #1

findings.title: Designing for an unknown or conditional cultural occupant
findings.summary: With no MOCA commitment, the brief offers three occupancy strategies and recommends a hybrid: flexible space with no MOCA-specific infrastructure, upgraded only if a partner commits.
details: - Option A (unknown occupant): 20-30K sq ft ground-floor space divisible into 2,000-3,000 sq ft modules; no gallery-specific loading, security or climate systems; adaptable to a nonprofit, archive, artist studios, a local history museum, or vacancy.
- Option B (expressed occupant): requires a signed MOCA board letter and a financial commitment before gallery-optimized design; risk of underused space if MOCA withdraws.

- Option C (cultural/community partner): an LOI with the Angels Flight Railway Foundation, local history groups or an independent curator; 20K sq ft permanent history exhibition plus 10K sq ft rotating.
The brief argues this is intellectually stronger: the space answers to the neighborhood rather than to a downtown institution with no historical tie to the site.

- Corrected from source file: the brief's premise says MOCA's 'Director vacant (8/25/2025)'. In fact Ann Goldstein has been interim director since Aug 18, 2025 (Johanna Burton left July 2025), with a permanent search ongoing.

sources.title: Y-1 Strategic Brief, Design Shift #2

findings.title: Entitlements start from zero: alternative program scenarios
findings.summary: With no recorded Development Agreement and a likely-lapsed tract map, the brief treats the new program as open and sketches three alternative mixes.
details: The brief calls the absence of vested approvals 'liberation': a new buyer can propose a different height, use mix, phasing (affordable units first), parking and ground-floor strategy without justifying departures from Angels Landing.
- Housing-First Tower: 600 units (450 market, 150 affordable); 20-30K sq ft cultural/community; 30K sq ft neighborhood retail; underground parking plus a podium.

- Mixed-Use Affordable Focus: 400 residential units at 40% affordable (the file says '240 units affordable', which is inconsistent with 40% of 400); 15K sq ft office; 40K sq ft community cultural; food hall; possibly 8-10 stories.

- Hybrid Cultural + Housing: if the Angels Flight Foundation or a history organization commits, a 25K sq ft exhibition and restoration workshop, 10K sq ft temporary exhibition, 400 units in 200K sq ft, and 40 parking spaces.
- 'VTT-82842-SL likely expired (3-4 year validity)' is the brief's inference with no named source; unverified.

sources.title: Y-1 Strategic Brief, Design Shift #4

findings.title: Affordability pro forma scenarios and the 'affordability cliff'
findings.summary: The brief models 25%, 35% and 50% affordability and argues that 50% needs a nonprofit or public development partner, not a conventional market-rate firm.
details: - 25%: 650 units (487 market / 163 affordable), FAR 7.5:1, about $1.2B cost, $400M HCD loan, $200M equity.
- 35%: 650 units (423 / 227), about $1.1B, $550M HCD loan, $150M equity.
- 50%: 500 units (250 / 250), FAR 5.8:1, about $800M, $700M HCD loan, $50M equity.

- Assumptions: $4,500/month market rent; $900/month affordable rent (60% AMI); $1.8M/unit development cost; HCD loan at 50-70% LTV, 1-2% interest; 9% LIHTC. All are the brief's own assumptions with no named source (unverified). The 60% AMI target differs from the WebSearch file's 70-80% AMI.

The 'cliff': at 50%, the project cannot support developer equity without $0 land cost, $200M+ in competitive 9% LIHTC allocations, or philanthropic/government capital. Suggested partners with affordable-housing expertise: LA Family Housing, BRIDGE Housing, Community Corp of Santa Monica, Related California. The brief also says the HCD loan process adds 6-12 months.
Ground-floor priority order: affordable-unit amenities and resident services first, community programming (meeting rooms, job training), then cultural/history use, then neighborhood retail.

sources.title: Y-1 Strategic Brief, Design Shift #5

findings.title: Ground floor as a permanent Bunker Hill history exhibition
findings.summary: The brief recommends a self-sustaining permanent local-history exhibition (Option 3), with flexible neutral space as the fallback, so the ground floor becomes an archive of neighborhood change.
details: - Option 1 (flexibility): 20-30K sq ft of neutrally serviced space with a flexible structural grid; nothing is wasted if no occupant appears, but it is optimized for nothing.
- Option 2 (partner-led): a signed LOI covering use, operations and revenue sharing before design is finalized; authentic, but tied to that partner.

- Option 3 (permanent exhibition): 15-20K sq ft on Bunker Hill, Angels Flight and local history, plus 5-10K sq ft rotating; independently curated; funded by admissions, endowment and grants; the file estimates a modest endowment of about $500K (unverified, no source).

The argument: an archive of neighborhood change is more intellectually coherent and more locally accountable than a trophy space for an external institution. If MOCA or the Angels Flight Foundation commits later, programming can be enhanced.

sources.title: Y-1 Strategic Brief, Design Shift #6

findings.title: Stakeholder map: verified vs. conditional stakeholders
findings.summary: The brief separates agencies with a definite role from parties whose role depends on commitments not yet made, and treats MOCA as conditional.
details: - Verified stakeholders: CRA/LA (owner; SLA decision-maker), HCD (affordability enforcement and loan provider), LA City Planning (entitlements), LADBS (building permits).

- Conditional stakeholders: MOCA (only if its board commits in writing); Angels Flight Railway Foundation (if a partnership is pursued); Bunker Hill residents and the local community; an affordable-housing development partner (if 35%+ affordability is pursued); geotechnical and title consultants.

- Engagement sequence: Year 1 scoping with CRA/LA, HCD and Planning plus archival, title and geotech work; Year 2 HCD financing talks and partner outreach; Year 3 full community engagement and a cultural partner LOI; Years 4-5 formal entitlements and LADBS.
- The obligations table also sets out a 'verify before locking in program' principle: 'Research findings drive program, not the reverse.'

sources.title: Y-1 Strategic Brief, Stakeholder Engagement Strategy

findings.title: Y-1's three-dimensional legal identity and title encumbrances
findings.summary: Y-1 is a residual made of a buildable lot, appurtenant easement rights and a non-insurable subsurface strip, so every section through the site crosses a different legal regime.
details: - Parcel 1 (buildable lot): Lot 5, Tract 30781. Three defensible, non-contradictory areas: 95,425 sq ft (LADBS, per title), 97,631 sq ft (2021 EIR), and about 104,947 sq ft including the vacated Olive Street right-of-way.
- Parcel 2 (easement rights): 1983 COREA with Bunker Hill Associates (see site-003).
- Parcel 3 (subsurface): vacated Olive Street ROW below 20 ft, noted as 'NOT an insurable parcel pursuant to Subdivision Map Act'.
- Mineral reservation: the title references the Bunker Hill Urban Renewal Project Area (Book M335 Page 106, recorded 1962).
- Early design question from the file: whether to design to the 95,425 sq ft lot or include the subsurface footprint, a difference the file puts at about 20,000-29,000 sq ft of FAR.

findings.title: Angels Flight right-of-way and Olive Street airspace carve-outs
findings.summary: Two recorded carve-outs cut into the buildable envelope: the Angels Flight Railway right-of-way (recorded Dec 22, 2017) and the airspace above 17 ft on Olive Street held by 2 Cal Land (recorded Nov 29, 2016).
details: Both carve-outs come from the title-based parcel description in Key Findings and are repeated in the WebSearch file.

- The Strategic Brief says to 'Preserve 30 ft right-of-way; no building zone' and to design with a '30 ft setback on Olive Street', while confirming there are no utility or foundation conflicts. The 30 ft dimension has no named source (unverified).
- The risk map rates the Angels Flight ROW as MEDIUM severity, to be resolved in Year 1.
- The Angels Flight history is also proposed as ground-floor exhibition content (see des-005).

findings.title: 1983 COREA easements with California Plaza remain unexamined
findings.summary: The recorded 1983 Construction, Operation & Reciprocal Easement Agreement (Instr. 83-991992) and its 1993 and 1997 amendments may constrain Y-1's envelope, utilities and uses, but no one has reviewed the full terms.
details: The COREA is described as the foundational document for California Plaza development and for Y-1's appurtenant easements. It is also a possible home for the unlocated 'local history museum' provision.
- Risk map: HIGH severity. Commission a title attorney to review the full COREA and identify impacts on the building envelope and utilities (Year 1).
- Open question in the WebSearch file: do California Plaza easements constrain Y-1 uses?
- Retrieval route: LA County Recorder, full text of Instr. 83-991992 and amendments; CRA/LA archives for copies and interpretations.

findings.title: Geotechnical hazards and insurability: landslide, liquefaction, grade fall
findings.summary: The site lies in both landslide and liquefaction zones and has a 70 ft fall from Olive St to Hill St, so a geotechnical report and insurance underwriting must come before permits and should shape the program.
details: - Risk map: landslide hazard zone rated HIGH (foundation strategy of piles vs. grade beams, seismic implications); liquefaction zone rated MEDIUM (needs structural engineer input on foundations and lateral bracing).
- The WebSearch file lists '70 ft excavation + site fall' among underwriting risks and asks about insurability and underwriting terms; insurance terms are unknown.

- The Validation Protocol calls for a preliminary geotech assessment: a review of USGS landslide and liquefaction maps, existing boring logs (for example from the Angels Landing EIR), foundation options, and liquefaction-induced settlement. It estimates 2-3 weeks and $3,000-5,000.

- It also calls for a preliminary title insurance commitment (First American, Chicago Title, Fidelity National, etc.) to identify non-insurable zones and whether earthquake, subsidence or liquefaction coverage is needed, at an estimated $0-500.
- The hazard-zone designations and the 70 ft figure appear without a specific named map or source (unverified).

findings.title: Zoning envelope: FAR 9:1 base, 13:1 bonus, uncapped height
findings.summary: The files report current zoning as [HB5-G1-5] [CX3-FA] [CPIO], a mixed-use district that fully enables a project on the scale of Angels Landing without a zone change.
details: - Form district High-Rise Broad (height uncapped, governed by FAR); General frontage (90% build-to on the primary street, 70% on the side); use district CX3 Commercial-Mixed Use; Downtown CPIO overlay.
- Base FAR 9.0:1 (about 859,000 sq ft as of right); bonus FAR 13.0:1 for affordable housing or public benefits (about 1,240,000 sq ft); minimum 10 stories; practical height about 850-900 ft.
- Mixed use (for example museum plus housing) is permitted. Any conflict between uses is practical, design or financial, not legal.

- Reconcile: the corrected research framework describes the parcel as C4 under the Bunker Hill Specific Plan (Ord. 182576), which permits mixed use. These files instead cite the new downtown code designation. Confirm which designation governs and when it took effect.

findings.title: Verify the 1980 'bargain' and whether it can be enforced
findings.summary: The protocol sets out archival and legal routes to find the 1980 master plan or confirm it is lost, and to get a written opinion on whether any Y-1 use restriction still binds.
details: - CCA (Montreal): request a search of AP022.S1.1979.PR07 (Erickson/California Plaza fonds: about 150 drawings, 1,120 slides, 3 models) for the brief, program requirements and covenants mentioning Y-1, museum, contingent use or reversionary rights. archives@cca.qc.ca, +1-514-939-7000; 3-4 weeks.
- LA County Recorder (Norwalk): title search of 1980-1983 recordings on the Y-1 APN for covenants or deed restrictions; cross-check against the 1983 COREA. 1-2 weeks, $5-20 per document.
- CRA/LA archives (555 S. Flower St, Suite 750): the 1959 Plan and amendments, the 1980 master plan, legal opinions on 'reserved use', board minutes 1980-2012.

- Legal opinion: a California redevelopment-law attorney on whether a restriction exists, whether it survives defunct counterparties and the 2012 dissolution, and what title insurance reveals. Estimated $2,000-3,500 over 4-6 weeks. Also ask CRA/LA General Counsel for the agency's own position.

- Decision rule: if found and binding, include cultural programming; if questionable, design for flexibility; if not found after a thorough search, treat it as a teaching premise and cultural use as optional.

findings.title: Verify California Plaza receivership and Bunker Hill Associates' status
findings.summary: The receivership claim and the 'untraceable' status of Bunker Hill Associates, L.P. both need primary-record confirmation before Insight 7 can be relied on.
details: - Receivership: search the LA Superior Court docket for a 2025 filing on 1 California Plaza; get the receiver appointment order, asset inventory and resolution timeline (about 1 week).

- Bunker Hill Associates, L.P.: search the CA Secretary of State business database and Dun & Bradstreet for dissolution date, final filings and successors; check the LA County Assessor for properties still in its name (1-2 days).

- The WebSearch file adds further leads: successors to Metropolitan Structures West (Secretary of State search) and individual partners of Bunker Hill Associates (SEC filings, prospectuses, archives).
- The Strategic Brief also suggests a title insurance consultation on what the receivership means for Y-1.

findings.title: Confirm Angels Landing Final EIR status and the CEQA path for a new project
findings.summary: Whether a Final EIR was issued and certified for ENV-2018-3273-EIR decides whether a new project can use an Addendum or Subsequent EIR or needs a new EIR; the files disagree on its status.
details: - Conflict: Key Findings says 'Final EIR status unknown' with no certification found, while the WebSearch file says 'Final EIR: Received May 27, 2021 (likely certified; exact certification date unconfirmed)'.
- CEQAnet (State Clearinghouse): list NOP, Draft EIR (Jan 2021), Final EIR and NOD filings under Bunker Hill, Y-1 and Angels Landing. https://ceqanet.opr.ca.gov; 1-2 weeks.

- LA City Planning (200 N. Spring St): meet the case manager for ENV-2018-3273-EIR; request the NOD and the Mitigation Monitoring Plan if certified; ask whether a new proposal takes the Addendum or SEIR path.
- The WebSearch file estimates 12-24 months for a new EIR (unverified). The risk map rates this item HIGH for Year 1.

findings.title: Verify MOCA's institutional interest in Y-1
findings.summary: The protocol proposes a MOCA development-office interview and a Form 990 review (2017-2026) to confirm or refute any board-level interest in Bunker Hill, with design decisions branching on the result.
details: - Interview: ask MOCA's Director of Development whether the board has considered or committed to Y-1, whether any capital campaign or downtown feasibility study exists, what would trigger downtown interest, and for board minutes from 2017-2026 (250 S. Grand Ave, +1-213-626-6222).

- Form 990 review via ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer: search for Bunker Hill, Y-1, Angels Knoll and downtown expansion; check Part VII for current leadership. (The file also lists GiveWell as a Form 990 source, which is questionable.)

- Outcomes: if MOCA commits (board approval plus capital campaign), optimize the ground floor for MOCA and treat it as a development partner, adding 3-4 months of coordination; if MOCA declines or stays silent, pursue the Angels Flight Foundation, a local history group, or an independent permanent exhibition.

- Corrected from source file: the protocol's premise and checklist state 'director position vacant' and 'MOCA director vacant since 8/25/2025'. In fact Johanna Burton left in July 2025 and Ann Goldstein has been interim director since Aug 18, 2025, with a permanent search ongoing. The checklist item should be restated as leadership in transition.

findings.title: Outstanding critical unknowns and the validation program
findings.summary: Several gating facts remain unknown across the files. The protocol budgets $15,000-25,000 and about 15 weeks of two-tier research to close them before the program is locked in.
details: - Unknowns: whether and when CRA/LA issued the Notice of Availability and who responded; the Angels Landing settlement terms and approval timing (PACER, Case 2:26-cv-01524, Sept 10 and 12, 2026 entries); VTT-82842-SL expiry and transferability; HCD's enforcement posture toward CRA/LA; whether the settlement favors any particular use.
- Also open: whether any off-site affordability option survives from the Angels Landing structure (Key Findings), and the WebSearch file's unexplained '25% or 50% on-site + 65 off-site' scenario.

- Program: Tier 1 archival and title research (Q4 2026-Q2 2027), Tier 2 interviews and legal review (Q2-Q3 2027), synthesis in Q4 2027. Budget: attorney $5-8K, archival $3-5K, geotech $5-7K, CEQA $2-4K (all the file's own estimates, unverified).

- Pro forma decision: if 35%+ affordability proves feasible with an HCD loan, tax credits and a nonprofit developer, recommend it; if only 25% works, design to the SLA floor with conventional HCD financing.
- Success criteria include a verification matrix at least 90% complete and CRA/LA alignment before design proceeds.
